turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Mrs Keane, before the doctor comes in, I've your blood pressure at one thirty eight over eighty two, and the pulse is 76. You can stay where you are.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine. I'm seventy four and I'm wrecked, so the sooner this is done the better.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hello there, I'm Dr Brennan. Come on in, the pair of ye. What's been troubling you, in your own words?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): The legs. At night they seize up in desperate cramps, and stretching or walking it off only helps a small bit. Next day I'm like a wet rag.
[SEG0005] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's roaring the house down some nights. Mam, tell her how long it's been.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, two months, maybe longer, I haven't a notion exactly. Both calves, the right is worse, and I'm too tired to be counting.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): Is it just the calf, or does it run up into the thigh as well?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Just the calf. I get up and stamp around the kitchen and—
[SEG0009] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And she won't drink. I put a glass by the chair and it sits there all day.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Will you let me finish. Then I can't get back to sleep, and I'm fit to be tied.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): The sleep is broken after them, I hear you. How much are you actually drinking in the day?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah, I don't... uh, the tea goes cold half the time.
[SEG0013] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Go on, Mam.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): A cup of tea in the morning and a sup of water with the tablet. That's the height of it.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any swelling in the ankles, pain in the chest, or getting short of breath?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None of that. Don't be adding things on me.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Grand, I won't pile on. What tablets are you taking at the minute?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): The water tablet. I call it frusamide, forty milligrams every morning, years now, for the blood pressure I think. And I got magnesium in the chemist for the cramps.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Frusemide forty milligrams each morning for the blood pressure, yes. The magnesium, what strength, and how often?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): One at night. The dose, err, I haven't a notion, the bottle's at home.

[SEG0021] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She doesn't always take that magnesium either. And Auntie Brid keeps pushing her biotin, the hair tablets, as if that'd fix cramps. Brid's the one on the biotin, not Mam.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): I take it most nights. I can't hear myself think with the two of ye going on. Brid's tablets are her own business.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Anything else, even now and again?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Two paracetamol, the 500 ones, if the legs are sore after a bad night. Not every day.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any reactions to medicines at all? Anything that didn't suit you?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm not... look, I'm wrecked, can we not—
[SEG0027] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He has to ask, Mam.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No, never. I've taken penicillin and everything, the amoxacillin one years back, and not a bother.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good, so nothing that disagreed with you. I'll have a look at the calves. They're soft, there's no heat, no swelling, and the pulses in both feet are there.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): They feel grand sitting here. It's only in the bed they go mad.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Apart from the legs and the tiredness, any bother with the tummy or the waterworks?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No. That's all grand. It's the cramps and being wrecked, nothing else.

[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): I think these night cramps may well be tied to the water tablet and you drinking so little, but I won't change the frusemide until we see the salts. I'll book bloods for the potassium, and the kidney numbers with them.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): More bloods. Brilliant. That's all I need.

[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): I know it's a nuisance. Stretch the calves before you get into bed, and try for more than that one cup of tea, even a glass with the dinner. We'll see you back in a fortnight with the results.
[SEG0036] person_1 (NURSE): I'll book the bloods for tomorrow morning at the desk, and the review for two weeks. Mind yourselves.

spec.situation: Older person with calf cramps at night for two months; takes a water tablet; drinks little water; magnesium from the shop; blood tests for potassium planned; stretching advice.

traps.happens: The doctor asks about drug reactions. Variants (use ONE per encounter): (a) the patient says 'No, never, I have taken penicillin and everything' (no allergy); (b) the patient is unsure ('maybe the antibiotic or the painkiller, nobody told me which'); (c) a real allergy with the reaction described; (d) allergies are never asked.
traps.label_rule: (a) NO allergy entry: negative_findings 'Allergies' absent. (b) allergy with status uncertain, the substance as described, the reaction if said, plus an allergy_uncertain uncertainty. (c) allergy with the reaction. (d) nothing at all. NEVER list a medicine the patient has taken without a reaction as an allergy, and the plan must not prescribe a drug of a recorded allergy's family.

traps.happens: The patient describes things in colourful or sentence-like speech ('I've overdone it', 'I can't hear myself think', 'a frog in my throat', 'my feet feel dead', 'I feel like a wet rag').
traps.label_rule: Every symptom name is a short clinical noun phrase of 1 to 5 words ('voice fatigue', 'numbness in both feet', 'tiredness'), never a full sentence, never starting with I/we/my. Pure idioms that are not symptoms ('I can't hear myself think' said about classroom noise) are NOT symptoms. The patient's own words stay in the cited turn, not in the name.

features: interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.

bad.reason: Hypertension implied by 'for the blood pressure' and 'years now'; not explicitly stated as diagnosed history.
Existing hypertension implied by medication being for blood pressure for years; diagnosis not explicitly named.

omissions.text: Doctor stated he would not change the frusemide until the blood salts/results are seen.
Patient denied thigh involvement; cramps are just in the calves and do not run up into the thigh.
Patient said the cramps occur only in bed / at night and the calves feel fine while sitting in the clinic.
Patient reported she cannot get back to sleep after the cramps.
Family member stated biotin is taken by Auntie Brid, not by the patient, clarifying the patient is not taking biotin.
Paracetamol dose is recorded incorrectly: patient takes two 500 mg tablets as needed (total 1000 mg per dose), not 500 mg.
Allergy history included specific tolerance: patient reported she had taken penicillin and amoxicillin previously without any problem.
Follow-up logistics were specified: nurse said bloods would be booked for tomorrow morning at the desk and the review booked for two weeks.
